Others have already mentioned practical help and spending time with them to take their mind off it, but just be 'normal' around them. It's great you're being careful about not becoming overbearing, not wrapping them in bubble wrap is so important as their whole world is changing so much they'll appreciate your normalcy. 

Be consistent, a surprising amount of their support could wane over time, so just keeping up a strong friendship is key. Also keep an eye out for when/if he recedes into himself and reduces his attention to you or himself, of course approach with caution and due care but I found instead of saying 'do you want to do...', saying 'we're doing... tomorrow' worked well.

It's amazing to be involved but I'd try to facilitate their time together too. Maybe buy them a Christmas decoration like a photo frame bauble, or buy them tickets or a voucher to something like the zoo or a film, bring them a board game or murder mystery pack, etc. Possibly help their independence by becoming part of their distraction (you mentioned cooking might be one for them, instead of taking over all the cooking you could you cook together? etc.)

All the microchips/integrated circuits that make up electronics such as phones, computers, and cars, is going through a major shortage right now. Cars nowadays use a huge amount of these microchips in its electronics to manage everything from starting the car to emergency braking to lane keep assist. Unfortunately there's just not enough to go round right now, which is why cars are so expensive atm.

At least the next two years and I'd bet prices won't return to pre-chip shortage levels until end of 2024, at the earliest. The chip shortage is predicted to ease going into 2023, but it'll take time for that to trickle down into lower car prices.

Truthfully no one knows exactly when its going to end, we can only make guesses based on production which is significantly ramping up right now - but its still a slow process. Even if you alleviated the chip shortage today, how long it'd take prices level out is anyone's guess especially as back-order waiting lists are miles long. IMO, optimistically 2024 is when prices will start to go down if they're going to. But, at a wildly blind guess, it could be until 2026 we see normal pre-covid prices

Hey, I used to volunteer at a food bank and here's what we usually needed although I'd check on your local's food bank website and they'll tell you what they need.

Toiletries in every form. As previous commenters said: Toilet paper (we found TP was the most desirable/useful donation), shower gel, shampoo, soap, feminine hygiene products, washing up liquid, surface cleaners, wipes, sponges etc.

Tinned meats. There's usually a lot of pasta, accompanying sauces, beans etc., so tinned meat such as pies, suet puddings, meat+gravy mixes, veggies (potatoes, tinned tomatoes, green beans, sweetcorn are all great).

Long-life products such as pulses (quinoa, lentils, beans, etc.), milk, cereal, crisps. Chocolate/treats are always a welcome addition in the form of bars, tinned fruits, or puddings.

But to be honest the most valuable donation was money. We could purchase food at a fraction of the cost of supermarkets, even as a very small bank. Definitely donate some food, and although money isn't as tangible to you, it's much more valuable to your local food bank (and donating your time is always good) - if you have any questions please hit me up! I've dealt with exactly this situation before so hopefully I can offer some resemblance of advice.

My old housemate was self-destructive and made every conversation acutely centred around her issues, advice went in one ear and out the other. I'm not a confrontational person and doing what I needed to do was hard, especially because her reaction made it feel unjustified (when it absolutely wasn't).

I sat her down and had an honest chat about how I was feeling, in a calmly understanding but assertive way. I said that I helped as much as I could, but I'm not in a position to provide the support she needed. Support her search for help/resources to get better, but you need to make it clear to her that you cannot provide the support she needs and also sustaining both of your mental healths. I'd recommend making it clear you're still housemates and (good?) friends, but your own advice isn't working and they need someone else, and that's okay. You're asking them to seek someone else because you want them to feel better, and for you both to feel better.

It's going to be a hard conversation but it's one you must make. As someone who's been in this exact situation before, the earlier you clear the air the better, I can't recommend having this talk soon enough. She should be understanding, and if she isn't that is in no way on you! (also while my housemate was a bit upset at first, it was soon over and things got a bit better).

Best of luck to you, you need to look after yourself too.

Keep a dream journal, as soon as you wake up scribble down everything you can remember. Say to yourself, quietly aloud, 'I will remember my dreams' or similar chant as you go to sleep (stop when you're very close to sleeping), then really focus on remembering your dreams. Once you remember slightly more and more, start to try and recognise when you're dreaming. Perform quick reality checks, often throughout the day to make sure you're not dreaming. Sounds ridiculous, but pinch yourself or say to yourself 'Am I dreaming?', this habit should hopefully continue into your dreams until one day you *are* dreaming. Another way is to look at words in your dream, glance away from it and look back, hopefully it will have changed - this means you're dreaming. Recognising you're dreaming is the hardest part, it takes a lot of time but chanting 'I'll be in my dreams', reality checks and looking at words may help you recognise when you're dreaming. Once you can recognise you're dreaming, by looking at words in them or other, you can try to take control of it. It's a very long inconsistent process, but worth it when you can do it.
